unit.unitOverview: Hello! I am Idris. I go to Ehel Academy in Hargeisa. In this unit we will find out what it means to be fair. Do these activities with your grown-up. Say your ideas out loud, take your time, and have fun! Some activities have a box to draw in, and some have questions to talk about. Every one of them helps you become a fairness expert.

explainers.title: 1. Is it fair?
explainers.body: Read each one with your grown-up. Put a tick if you think it is fair. Put a cross if you think it is not fair. Then say why. Remember, there is no wrong answer if you can give a reason!

rows: Two friends share a mango. One gets a big piece. The other gets a tiny bit.
Everyone in the game gets a turn to play.
A farmer works hard growing bananas but is not paid enough to buy food.
A shop pays a coffee farmer a fair price for her coffee.
One child must tidy the whole room while the others play.
Idris and Amal both get the same time on the swing.

explainers.title: 2. Needs and wants
explainers.body:
A need is something we must have to live, like food and water. A want is something nice we would like, but do not need. Read the list below, then write or draw each thing in the right box. Some are easy, and some might make you think!

The things to sort: water, a toy car, food, a home, sweets, clean clothes, a games machine, love and care, a fancy phone, going to school.

explainers.title: 3. Draw a fair-trade food
explainers.body: Fair trade means the farmer gets a fair price for their hard work. Many foods can be fair trade. Draw your favourite fair-trade food in the box, then write its name. Is it a banana, coffee, honey, sesame, a mango, or dates? Think about which fair-trade foods you have tasted before. Which one is your favourite?

explainers.title: 4. The banana's journey
explainers.body:
How does a banana get all the way from the farm to you? These steps are mixed up! Talk with your grown-up and write 1, 2, 3, 4 in the brackets to put them in the right order.

Now draw the journey as a little comic strip on another sheet of paper. Show the farmer, the fair price, the long trip, the shop, and you at the end!
bullets: The bananas travel a long way in a truck and on a boat. (____)
The farmer grows the banana plants in the warm sun. (____)
You buy the ripe banana at the shop. (____)
The farmer picks the ripe bananas and is paid a fair price. (____)

explainers.title: 5. My fair-trade questions
explainers.body: Answer these with your grown-up. You can say them out loud or write a few words. Take your time and think.
bullets: What does the word 'fair' mean to you?
Name one thing that is a need.
Name one thing that is a want.
What is fair trade? Try to say it in one sentence.
Why is a fair price good for the farmer?

explainers.title: 6. Being fair at home
explainers.body: Being fair is not only about faraway farmers. We can be fair every single day, right here at home. Think of one fair and kind thing you could do this week. Maybe you could share your toys, take turns with a friend, or help someone without being asked. Draw or write your fair idea in the box.

headers: My fair idea for this week

explainers.title: 7. Two friends, two ideas
explainers.body:
Idris asked two friends the best way to help people who do not have much. They did not agree! Read what they each said. Who do you agree with more? Put a tick by one, and tell your grown-up why.

There is no wrong answer. Both friends want to help, they just have different ideas. Can you think of a time when each idea would be the best one?
bullets: Amal says: 'Giving to charity is the best way to help. People get what they need quickly.' (____)
Sami says: 'It is better to help people earn their own money, so they can always buy what they need.' (____)

explainers.title: My new words
explainers.body:
These are the words you have been learning in this unit. How many can you use today? Point to each one and try to tell your grown-up what it means.

Well done for finishing your Activity Sheet! You are getting really good at spotting what is fair and what is not. Keep asking that special question: is it fair? And keep saying why!

models.title: How Idris began his poster
lines: Idris chose to make a poster for the shopkeeper near his home in Hargeisa.
At the top he wrote in big letters: Please sell fair-trade food!
He drew a smiling banana farmer being paid a fair price for her bananas.
At the bottom he wrote: I think fair trade is good, because the farmer can then send her children to school.
Now it is your turn. What will your letter or poster say?
You can borrow Idris's idea, or make up your very own. Your poster can be about bananas, coffee, honey, sesame, or any fair-trade food you like best.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor (with a grown-up)
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor with your grown-up. Tell it: I am learning about fair trade.
Ask it: can you name a food that can be fair trade?
Ask it: why is it kind to pay a farmer a fair price for their hard work?
Talk about the answer together. Do you agree with the tutor? Why?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor (with a grown-up)
lines: With your grown-up, tell the AI tutor what your letter or poster is about.
Ask it: can you help me think of one more kind reason to buy fair-trade food?
Ask it: are my words clear and easy for people to understand?
You choose what to use and what to change. It is your project!

speakingPrompts.title: Idris says
lines: There are no wrong answers here, as long as you can say why you think so.
The best thinkers use one special word again and again. That word is because!

speakingPrompts.title: Before you start
lines: This is your project, so pick the idea you like best.
Do not worry about making it perfect. A bright, happy, honest poster is the best kind.
Take your time. You can make it over two or three days.

grownUpGuide.label: For the grown-up
grownUpGuide.intro: This part is written for the parent or teacher sitting with the learner, and is kept in their own words.

sections.title: Hello, and welcome to this unit
sections.body:
Hello, and welcome to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. This guide is written for you, the grown-up, whether you are a teacher in a class or a parent at home. You will lead these lessons together with your child, side by side.

Global Perspectives is a little different from other subjects. It is not about learning long lists of facts. It is about growing thinking skills that a child will use for the whole of their life. In this unit, the topic is fairness, but the real gift is helping your child learn to think, to compare, and to give reasons.

The big question of this unit is simple but powerful: what does it mean to be fair? Along the way your child will explore needs and wants, and a kind idea called fair trade — the idea that the farmers who grow our food should get a fair price for their hard work.

sections.title: The thinking skills your child will build
sections.body:
In Global Perspectives we say the topic is the vehicle, and the thinking skill is the destination. Fairness is our topic this time, but these are the skills we are quietly growing in a 7 to 8 year old:

These are the small seeds of the six big Global Perspectives skills that grow in later years: research, analysis, evaluation, reflection, collaboration and communication. You do not need to teach those big words now. Just help your child look, compare, and say what they think and why.

You will see these skills appear in the lessons as three friendly questions you can ask again and again: 'What is the same and what is different?' for comparing, 'Is that fair?' for judging, and 'Why do you think that?' for giving reasons. If you ask nothing else all unit, ask these three.
items: Comparing — noticing what is the same and what is different, such as a need compared with a want, or something fair compared with something not fair.
Judging what is fair — looking at a real situation and deciding if it is fair, and beginning to say why.
Giving reasons — using the words 'I think ... because ...' to explain an opinion out loud.

sections.title: How these lessons work (the Ehel way)
sections.body: At Ehel Academy, young learners are guided by a grown-up. Three kinds of support work together, and you are the one who ties them all together:
items: You lead, together. You and your child read the simple, picture-led activities and talk about them. Keep each lesson short and gentle, about 15 to 20 minutes. Stop when your child is tired, and come back to it later.
A teacher session about twice a week. Your child meets their Ehel Academy teacher to share their work, play a game, and talk with other children. Bring along whatever your child has made.

An AI tutor, used with a grown-up. A few activities say 'Ask Your AI Tutor (with a grown-up)'. This is a friendly helper you use together. You sit with your child, you type or read the questions, and you talk about the answers as a pair.

sections.title: Meet the children in this unit
sections.body:
To make the ideas warm and real, a few children appear again and again. You can point to them as you read:

There is no need to remember them all. They are simply friendly faces to make the talking easier.
items: Idris is our main friend. He is in Year 3 at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa. He is doing a school project about being fair, and he loves to ask questions.
Amal and Karim are Idris's friends. They help him think, and they do not always agree, which is a good thing.
Sami has his own way of looking at things and often asks, 'but is that really fair?'
Amara is a girl whose family are banana farmers. The children read her true-feeling story to understand how fair trade can change a family's life.

sections.title: Key words for this unit
sections.body: Here are the important words, in simple language. Teach them slowly, one or two at a time, as they come up. There is a child-sized word box in the Activity Sheet too.

rows: Treating people in the right way, so everyone has what they need.
Things we must have to live, like food, clean water, a home and love.
Nice things we would like, but do not need to live, like toys or sweets.
Things that are grown or made to be sold, like food or clothes.
When farmers and workers in poorer places get a fair price for their hard work.
Paying enough money so the farmer can buy what their family needs.
Giving money, things or time to help people who need it.
A group of farmers who work together and help each other.
A person who knows a lot about something.

sections.title: What you will need
items: The Activity Sheet and the Mini-Project & Reflection sheet (print them if you can).
Paper, and coloured pencils or crayons.
Scissors and glue, if you have them (helpful but not needed).
If you can, one real fair-trade food to look at and hold, such as a banana, a packet of coffee, honey, sesame, or dates. Look for a fair-trade mark on the packet.
A device with the AI tutor, for a few short moments together.

sections.title: A few tips for leading these lessons
sections.body: You know your child best. Still, these small habits help the lessons go well with 7 and 8 year olds:
items: Read with feeling. Put on different voices for Idris, Amal and Sami. Your child will lean right in.
Ask more than you tell. A good question, such as 'what do you think?', teaches more than a fact ever could.
Wait after you ask. Count slowly to five in your head. Young thinkers need a little quiet time to find their words.
Praise the reason, not just the answer. Say 'I love that you gave a reason,' even when you see it differently.
Use real things. A real banana or a coffee packet on the table makes fair trade come alive.
Keep it kind. If your child says something that sounds unfair, do not scold. Gently ask them to think about it again.

sections.title: How to run the six little lessons
sections.body: Here are six short lessons, in order. Spread them over about two to three weeks and go at your child's pace. Each one has an Aim (what it is for), a Talk about (a gentle chat), and a Do (a small activity). Some point to the Activity Sheet.

sections.title: Lesson 1 - What does fair mean?
sections.body:
Aim: to help your child feel what the word 'fair' means.

Talk about: Take a snack you can share, such as a mango or some bread. Share it two ways: first give one person a big piece and the other a tiny piece, then share it evenly. Ask: which way felt fair? Why? Talk about times at home or school that felt fair or not fair.

Do: Together, do the 'Is it fair?' activity in the Activity Sheet. Then meet the word charity — giving money, things or time to people who need it. Many families, whether they go to the mosque or the church, teach that sharing and being fair to others is important. Share two friendly views: Amal thinks charity is the very best way to help people in need, because they get what they need quickly. Sami thinks it is even better to help people earn their own money, so they can always buy what they need. Ask your child who they agree with. There is no wrong answer here.

sections.title: Lesson 2 - What do you need?
sections.body:
Aim: to tell the difference between needs and wants.

Talk about: What must we have to stay alive and well? These are needs: food, clean water, a home, clothes, and people who love us. What is only nice to have? These are wants: toys, sweets, games. Wants are lovely, but we can live without them.

Do: Do the 'Needs and wants' sort in the Activity Sheet together. Then read Amara's story in the box below, slowly and with feeling. Talk about how the charity's food helped Amara's family for a short time, but the banana plants and the cooperative helped them for a long time.

sections.title: Lesson 3 - What is fair trade?
sections.body:
Aim: to learn what fair trade means.

Talk about: First, the word trade — it just means buying and selling things. When Idris buys a banana, that is trade. Now ask: is the farmer who grew the banana being treated fairly? Do they get enough money for all their hard work?

Do: Start a simple KWL chart together on a sheet of paper. Make three columns: K for what we Know, W for what we Want to know, and L for what we have Learned. Write one thing in each. Then teach the key idea below. Fair-trade foods your child may know include bananas, coffee, honey, sesame, mangoes and dates — many grown by farmers in East Africa and other warm places. Keep this chart on the wall or in a folder, and add to the 'Learned' column all through the unit. It is lovely to watch it fill up.

sections.title: Lesson 4 - What fair-trade foods can we buy?
sections.body:
Aim: to find out which foods can be fair trade.

Talk about: Which foods might travel a long way from a farm to reach us? Bananas, coffee, honey, sesame, mangoes, dates, and chocolate are all foods that can be fair trade. Look at any packets you have at home for a fair-trade mark.

Do: Play a quick game of 'Draw it!' — one person draws a fair-trade food and the other guesses it. Then, if you like, make a simple home-made board game together: draw a winding path of squares on a big sheet, write a happy fair-trade step on some squares (such as 'you sell your bananas for a fair price, move on 2') and a setback on others (such as 'a storm hurts your crop, wait a turn'), and use a coin or a stone as a counter. Add any new words to your KWL chart. Introduce the word expert — your child is becoming a real fair-trade expert!

sections.title: Lesson 5 - The journey (from farm to you)
sections.body:
Aim: to see how a fair-trade food travels from the farmer all the way to us.

Talk about: Pick one food, such as a banana. Where does it grow? Who picks it? How does it travel to the shop near you? A banana may grow on a farm near a river, be picked by a farmer, be packed into a box, ride on a truck, cross the sea on a big ship, and only then reach the shop. So many hands help along the way, and the unit keeps asking: was the farmer at the very start paid fairly?

Do: Draw the journey together as a little comic strip, using the journey activity in the Activity Sheet. Show the farmer growing the plant, picking the fruit, being paid a fair price, the food travelling far, the shop, and finally your child buying it. This drawing can grow into the Final Task, so keep it safe.

sections.title: Lesson 6 - Do you agree about fair trade?
sections.body:
Aim: to begin to form an opinion and give a reason for it.

Talk about: Do lots of people know about fair trade? Do a tiny survey together: ask a few family members or neighbours, 'Have you heard of fair trade?' Count how many say yes and how many say no. Is that good, or not so good? Why?

Do: Read two or three simple opinions about fair trade with your child. For example: 'Buying fair-trade food is a lovely way to make the world fairer,' and 'Fair-trade food can cost a bit more, so some people are not sure.' Ask your child: do you agree or disagree? Why? Help them practise saying 'I think ... because ...'. Remind your child that people can disagree and still be friends. In Global Perspectives we listen kindly to views that are different from our own, and we never make fun of anyone for thinking differently.

sections.title: The Final Task
sections.body:
The unit ends with a small, joyful project. Your child makes a simple letter or poster (or a short video, if you prefer) about being fair, or about fair trade. The aim is to gently persuade someone to buy or sell fair-trade food, so that farmers get a fair price.

Full child-sized steps are in the Mini-Project & Reflection sheet. Help with the writing and the spelling, but let the ideas and the pictures be your child's own. This is where all six lessons come together.

Do not worry about making it perfect. A wobbly, honest poster made by a proud child is worth far more than a neat one made mostly by a grown-up. Your job is to help, to spell the tricky words, and to cheer. If your child would rather make a short video than a poster, that works just as well.

sections.title: Reflection - How did we do?
sections.body:
When the project is finished, sit together and look back. There is a simple 'How did we do?' checklist in the Mini-Project & Reflection sheet, with faces to colour. Ask your child what they enjoyed most, what was tricky, and who they asked for help. Then celebrate what they made. Looking back and thinking about our own learning is itself a skill, and it grows every time you do it.

You might also look back at the KWL chart your child started in Lesson 3. What did the 'Learned' column gain over the unit? Reading it back together shows your child, in their own words, just how much they now know. That proud feeling of 'I have learned so much!' is exactly what we are hoping for.

sections.title: A gentle note on talking about fairness
sections.body:
Some children may notice that some families have more than others. Keep the tone warm and hopeful. Focus on what we can do — share, be kind, be fair, and choose fair-trade food when we can — rather than on what anyone lacks. Take care never to make a child feel bad about what their own family has or does not have. If a child shares something personal, simply listen kindly. Being fair starts with being gentle with each other, right here in the room.

Thank you for giving your child this time. The habits they build here — looking closely, comparing fairly, and saying 'I think, because' — will help them for many years, in every subject and far beyond school. Enjoy the unit together.

project.title: Mini-project
project.intro: You have learned so much about being fair! You know about needs and wants, and you know about fair trade. Now you will make something to help other people be fair too. A grown-up will help you, but the ideas are all yours. Making something to share your ideas is one of the best ways to learn. Are you ready? Let's begin!

steps.title: Choose
steps.intro: Will you make a letter, a poster, or a video? Talk about it with your grown-up, then circle your choice: letter / poster / video. A poster is great for a wall or a shop window. A letter is great for one special person. A video is fun if you like to talk and act. Pick the one that feels best for you.

steps.title: Who is it for?
steps.intro: Who will you show it to? It could be a parent, a shopkeeper, your teacher, or your whole class. Think about who could really buy or sell fair-trade food. Write their name here: ______________________.

steps.title: What will you say?
steps.intro: Use these sentence starters to help you. Say them out loud first, then write them down or turn them into pictures. You do not have to use all of them — just the ones you like best.
items: Being fair is important because ...
The world is not always fair because some people do not have enough ...
Have you heard about fair trade? Fair trade is ...
You can buy or sell fair-trade food, like bananas, coffee or honey.
This helps farmers because ...
I think fair trade is good because ...

steps.title: Make it
items: Plan first. What pictures will you draw? Where will the words go? Use the whole sheet of paper.
Draw big, bright pictures of fair-trade foods, like bananas, coffee, honey or sesame.
Write your words neatly. Check your spelling with your grown-up.
Add lots of colour to make it bright and happy, so people want to look at it.

steps.title: Share it
steps.intro: Now share your work! Show your letter or poster to the person you chose. Read it out to them in a clear, proud voice. Then ask them a question: will you buy fair-trade food when you can? Listen kindly to what they say. Sharing your ideas so other people understand them is a wonderful skill. Be proud of your work!

reflection.prompt: Now let's look back at what you made. Read each line with your grown-up. For each one, tick a box: 'Yes!', 'A bit', or 'Not yet'. Being honest is a real strength, and it helps you do even better next time.
What did you enjoy most about making your letter or poster?
What was the trickiest part, and how did you get through it?
Did you ask anyone for help? Who did you ask?
Were you happy with what you made? Why, or why not?
What is one new thing you can do now that you could not do before?

assessment.note: Stages 1-3 are assessed through the mini-project and the look-back grid; the source pack ships no quiz.
